phase1.intro:
Take a breath — Unit 3's the one where your programs stopped assuming everything goes right.

Where do you want to start the recap?

topics.buttonText: How did the exception half of the unit fit together?
dialogue: [[term:try-catch-finally]] is the actual catching mechanism, [[term:throw]] creates one exception right now while [[term:throws]] just declares a possibility, and custom exceptions (extends Exception for checked, extends RuntimeException for unchecked) let you invent error types specific to your program's domain.

stickyNote.flavor: 🧵 catching, raising, declaring, and inventing your own
stickyNote.definition: try-catch-finally catches, throw raises, throws declares, and custom exceptions (extends Exception/RuntimeException) invent domain-specific errors.

topics.buttonText: How did all the I/O layers connect?
dialogue: The I/O half moved through layers, each wrapping the last: byte streams for raw binary data, character streams for text with encoding, buffered streams wrapping either to cut disk trips, and PrintWriter for convenient formatted output. Then File and NIO's Path/Files, and Serialization for saving whole objects. CSV tied it all together as one real-world format.

stickyNote.flavor: 🧱 layers wrapping layers, from raw bytes to CSV
stickyNote.definition: Byte streams → character streams → buffered streams → PrintWriter, plus File/NIO for file objects and Serialization for whole objects — CSV combines them all.

topics.buttonText: What's the mindset worth carrying forward?
dialogue: [[warn:The mindset worth carrying forward more than any single class name]]: [[key:assume the file might not be there, the input might be wrong, the disk might be full — and build for that reality instead of hoping around it]]. An empty catch block that swallows an exception silently is almost always worse than a loud crash.
Next up: Unit 4, Collections & Threads — organizing data at scale, and doing more than one thing at once.

stickyNote.flavor: 🛡️ build for failure instead of hoping around it
stickyNote.definition: The real lesson: assume files might be missing, input might be wrong, and build for that — an empty, silent catch block is worse than a loud crash.

phase1.openingDialogue: Unit 3 was about surviving when trust in the world turns out to be misplaced — exceptions, I/O layers, and a defensive mindset. 🛡️

phase2.openingDialogue: Two habits worth locking in before Unit 4~

phase3.openingDialogue: Final check! What makes code robust? 🤔

mcq.question:
Which practice makes a program MORE robust?

A) Using empty catch blocks to ignore all exceptions
B) Checking for null before accessing objects
C) Reading one byte at a time from a large file
D) Not closing files after use
E) Using System.out.println() for all errors

Select the BEST practice.

phase5.trivia: [[fun:Fun fact]]: the "never leave a catch block empty" advice is old enough to have its own well-known nickname among Java developers — "exception swallowing" — and static analysis tools like SonarQube and even some IDEs flag empty catch blocks as a code smell by default, precisely because they're one of the most common ways real production bugs go undiagnosed for months.
